Things had begun to change around, was coming into the 30s or late 29s, about that time. I mean, yeah.

Was your father like a real sharp guy? I mean, was this considered, like this barbershop quartet? Was it pretty, you know, hot stuff for that particular period? You know, did they think of it as, you know, kind of being on the, you know, the leading edge of music? Did they think it was pretty exciting to be doing? Was it?

Well, I think it was exciting to them in a way, but it was sort of common in New Orleans because people were singing and playing music or played piano, and so music was just another thing around. Yeah, right. Nobody really thought that this was great or that was great because it was every day, practically something was going on.
Everybody was doing something.
And so you were just surrounding my music all the time.
What did your father do for a profession? What was his...

Well, he worked in an ice house. It was an ice, what you call an ice pusher. These are guys that, when the three or four hundred pounds of ice would come out in a block, it'd come down the chute, and he would catch it with the ice hooks and raise it up there and stack it and put it in the ice house
there in that packing place there. Must have been a big guy.
No, he was about 180 pounds, but he was strong. He was a strong man. He used to lift the 400 pounds of ice up,
just grab it on the chute and lift it right up. And what about your mother?

My mother, she came from Algiers, Louisiana. She was born in Algiers, Louisiana and all the family. And they knew the Red Allen, they knew the Allen family over there. She knew Red Allen and all the... his father and all the Allen family. And she used to speak of old man Allen. Yeah. And she used to tell us many things, but she was a housewife.
Yeah. And so where did they meet? How did your family, your folks meet?

I think my father went to Algiers over there to either see a baseball game or something happened over there that he was over there at that time and he met my mother. During that time, he used to have little dances, go on and things like that. So they met in Algiers and they married in New Orleans. They came over this time. After my grandmother died, my mother moved to New Orleans with her aunt. And that's when my father married my mother in New Orleans.

So here you were, this little kid, George, listening to this barbershop quartet in the other room, your dad on the radio. Was the first instrument, you started to play the trumpet? Was that your first?
No, the first instrument was a bugle.
Yeah.
How did you get that? That was about 1925. And my instructor was Preci and Willie Humphrey's grandfather.
Really?
And Preci instructed me on the bugle because Preci used to sort of sidekick for the grandfather.
Yeah.
And my late, my brother, the late Raymond Fleming was playing the flute and I blew the bugle. So they had a drumming bugle corps at that time. Yeah.
In your house.
No, that was at the Tribune. We used to go around there to practice.
Well, what did Willie tell you about playing the, or Percy, what did they tell you about playing the bugle? You know, there you were. How old were you
when you started playing the bugle?
Pardon? How old were you?
Oh, let me see, 19. That was about nine years old. So you're nine years old and it was Percy Humphrey's.
What did Percy tell you? I mean, were the lessons he gave you then applicable to what you're playing now?

Well, not really. They showed me how to lift the horn, how to put it to my mouth and how to make a sound through the buzz system and a vibration. And from then on, they taught us how to play little songs, you know, that went along with the bugle.
Yeah.

In later years, I developed a way how to blow a C scale on the bugle. So I was playing songs like, ain't gonna rain no more no more and things like that. I was blowing that on the bugle and a lot of other songs. So they had a waffle man. Later, he went on the R-K circuit and my uncle used to pray every time he heard the waffle man come by, we'd have a jam session. He says, I have a nephew out here could blow with it. So we'd stand out in Washington Street there and maybe a clower in Washington and he would blow the bugle and I would blow the bugle and we'd have a jam session.
Well, what's the waffle man?

He was a guy that had a stove and a wagon and he had his wagon made into, like a kitchen and he used to drive around all day selling hot waffles and he'd make the, had the waffle iron and those things in his wagon and the coal fired and then people would buy that, say for five cents they'd get maybe six waffles.
Yeah, five cents for six waffles.
Yeah.
Yeah, not bad. But what was his bugle for?
Just an attraction, just an attraction. Yeah. He was an advertisement. People would blow, you know, blow the bugle. They knew the sound of the bugle. They knew he was nearby.
And so you would go out and play with the waffle guy? Yeah. With the waffle man?
Yes.
Yeah, that's great. You were the waffle man. Did he like seeing you?
Oh, we had a ball.
Yeah?
Yes, he liked to play with me and I learned a lot from him also.
Really?
Yes, I did. What did you learn
from the waffle man?

Well, tunes that he would play that I would pick him up by ear and then I would practice them. Next time, he'd come around, maybe it might have been two weeks, maybe a month, I'd have that tuned on so we would jam on that tune.
What tune? Like,

what tunes did the waffle man play? Well, like one of them, I said, like the, I remember, I ain't gonna run around no more and then we'd play, like we'd take certain parts in the key of, say, B flat, which used to be a key of C for maybe a B flat bugle and anything that was near that in that key of C for the bugle, we'd kind of jam if it's no more than four medges on it, you know. We'd jam right on the four medges or the eight medges, whatever, it would go in without the chains, too many changes and we'd just stay right in there and blow.
When you say jam, you mean just improvising?
Yes.
Yeah. So, how long did you play, when did you, you went from the bugle to the trumpet?

Yes. Why did you do that? after the band, they broke up the band from the Item Tribune, well, they had two bands, the white band was big, was a huge band and they had trumpets and everything in that, they had a real big band
Yeah.
And after that, the Tribune dissolved the band.
And you had a band, you were in a band.

Yeah, I was in the drum and bugle corps. Right. They had two bands and I was in the, we was in the, the all black drum and bugle corps. Yeah. So after that, I think it lasted about a year. Uh-huh. And after that, it was, it was not until, oh, about 1930 that I started playing the trumpet. And I saw an old trumpet that I bought for a few dollars and started, oh, beat up horn and started playing. Yeah. on it in about 1930.
Where did you see this trumpet? Where was it?
It was in a pawn shop and I think I paid about, oh, $15 for it at that time.
Why did you get it? money. I mean, why did you?

Well, I always wanted to play a trumpet. Louis Armstrong inspired me very much and they had other trumpet players like my mother used to tell us about Buddy Bolden, how he used to play the horn and how for my, for many blocks around you could hear him playing. And so, I've always wanted to play some kind of instrument.
Yeah.
And when Louis Armstrong came around and started blowing why he inspired me a lot.
Was that, did you just hear him on records, Louis?
Yes, yes.
Or was he, did he have a, was he in town at all or was it just the fact that these recordings were made and you heard him?

Yes, I used to hear him on the old 78s and I also heard King Oliver and, and on a lot of music because my father used to play the old 78 records. He had a lot of 78 records with blues by Betsy Smith, Mamie Smith, Ida Cox and all these singers.
Yeah.
And, and I used to hear them all the time and when I hear the trumpet why I like that better than the rest of the instruments.
Why was it, you know, Louis just seems to have affected everybody very strongly. What, what was it about Louis playing that got you?

Well, he revolutionized the whole idea of trumpet playing. In fact, his, his theory and everything was just different. He had a new approach to the part way it was something exciting about his high notes, something exciting about the singing because this is the first time anyone did the scat singing or singing in a deep voice like he had and got away with it. So he just put a new idea to the trumpet playing and the singing.
So you went out and you bought this trumpet in the pawn shop and how did you start? Did you take lessons or did you just figure it out yourself?

I just figured it out myself. And I was blowing around and I played with, during that time before I learned how to read, was playing with guys like Alfred Williams. And so Alfred Williams and I played with Steve Lewis, piano player. We played at the place, at the Saint-Sou Hall on Howard Street between Washington and 6. I played there with him and I was just, oh, I was about, oh, my teens, late teens at that time.
Yeah.
And,
Where'd you get the guts to do this? I mean, you never took a lesson on the trumpet and yet suddenly you're out there playing? Did you feel

self-conscious about it? It was later on that Alfred Williams said, well, George says, told my mother, say, this youngster's playing a hell of a lot of horn and he don't know how to read. So we better, I better take him to a guy who will teach him how to read. So he brought me to Manuel Perez. There was a Manuel Puri and a Manuel Perez. Well, I went to both of them and Manuel Perez was the one that taught me how to read between those two.
How do you spell his name?
P-O-R-E-E, Puri, and the other one is P-E-R-E-Z.
Yeah, but you studied with both of them. The one who taught you how to read was... Yeah.
So I took a few lessons and the rest of it I figured it out for myself.
Yeah.

And so that was about 1930, 31 I started and, you know, about 31 I started reading and 33 I had it pretty well done. You did? Yeah. Yeah. Well, I went on the Steamer Captain by that time. That was my first big job.
Yeah. Before you went on the Steamer Captain though, were you rubbing shoulders? Were there a lot of musicians around that you really admired that you, you know, you hung out with or you watched?
Oh, yes, yes.
Who was around then?
Well, there was Gene, where are you Gene? Where are you? A trumpet player, a great trumpet player.
Yeah, you've mentioned him a lot to me.
Oh, he was wonderful.
Yeah.
And he was playing either at the Fern or the Levita.
Uh-huh.

And Jim Robison and George Lewis was playing. One of them was playing at the Fern, the other one was playing at the Levita, whether it was Jim Robison or all of it. Well, now they had Joe Robichaux in the band with Gene Ware and I don't remember the other guy but I do remember Joe Robichaux was playing. No, it was not Joe Robichaux. I'm sorry about that.
Yeah.

It was a guy by the name that had two, we used to call him Gene but his name was Eugene Hall and Eugene Ware. He was the piano man. Oh, he was a good pianist. And they had a guy by the name of Bucket was playing drums at that time. And so I used to go down there and those guys played such long hours until they was glad to see anybody because they had a horn come in to give them a little relief.
Yeah, right.

So he would have his program and they always had sheet music. They were good musicians and he would teach me, he would show me how to do this. Well, you do this and you play this and you play that. I'll play it down once and I had a goodie at that time and then he would play it down and he'd show me how to play and through my ear and my little spelling and I'd begin to get familiar with music. And it was there, it was shortly, I used to go down there every night and then I'd go next door and hear George Lewis and Jim Robinson. Then I'd sit in there for a while and after I leave there, maybe the next night I would go up to Percy Humphrey, he was playing on Connell Street and he was playing what we call a jitney dance also, all these three bands. And I would go on Connell Street up there with him and then I'd play up there sometime with him.

You said they had sheet music, you know, all those bands that we hear now, you know, they made these records in the late, in the 60s, the late 50s, 60s, 70s, the kind of preservation hall bands. Were they playing the same kind of music then or was it much more arranged?

Well, before then they were playing more traditional jazz and the sheet music brought a lot of modern playing in. Like I remember like during that time Fletcher Henderson was arranging for Paul Whiteman. Yeah, it was Fletcher Henderson and a guy by the name of Don Redmond made a lot of Paul Whiteman's arrangements and Fletcher Henderson rather was arranging for Benny Goodman and then they had the music started, we started, I would start it rather playing sheet music like they had one of the pieces I remember was made popular was Josephine.
Yeah.
They had this guy playing alto playing Josephine and what was his name? I can't forget his name right there but he was playing that tune I thought Rudy Vallée. I was just curious

were these real tight arrangements because later these guys just sort of jammed they played tunes like Careless Love and they just seemed to kind of you know play them pretty loosely but in those days was it much more heavily arranged? Was the music much tighter?
No, I think it was more heavily arranged later on than it was during that time.
Oh, so it was pretty loose so you could sit in and

Well, to a certain extent you could sit in. Yeah. Some of the music some of the things wasn't as complicated as it become later on but some of the pieces were more complicated than their pieces later on say in the 30s such as High Society was one of the major pieces for a clarinet to play and if he couldn't go he couldn't go through the playing of the solo like Alfonso Picou like he played it then when he did learn that solo and could play it well he graduated as a clarinet player but until then he was just another man around trying to learn clarinet.
So, you got your first job on what which boat was it? Steamer Capital. Steamer Capital? Yeah. Yeah.
Capital.
And how'd you get the job and what happened? Where'd you play?

Well, I was recommended by the same guy Alfred Williams which was very instrumental in my welfare and so he recommended me to Sidney Desmond he says I have a How do you spell Sidney's name? S-I-D-N-E-Y D-I-S-V-I-G-N-E Uh-huh. And I played with him I mean I was Alfred introduced me to Sidney Desmond after he had told Sidney Desmond to come and listen to me play.
Right.
And after Sidney heard me play why Sidney invited me to a rehearsal at that time he was getting his band ready to go on the Steamer Capital and I went to a rehearsal once and he said well you're in.
That was it?

Yes. Although it was pretty rough I had a pretty tough time with the special arrangements because this was my first time playing special arrangements and they had a guy by the name of Rene there was another Rene Hall and this Rene Hall is a ghetto player and he was a very very good musician and he was arranging music from the Duke Ellington era and during that time there was Black and Tain Fantasy was one of these things
so it was getting a little more elaborate

yes well they put that up there and say hey you played Black and Tain Fantasy so this was something new to me I wasn't familiar with the arrangement the special arrangement but with the help of Gene Ware and Louis Nelson Trombone he helped me and with their help then I made it
what do you mean they'd help you

well they showed me how to read these things they showed me how to say attack certain notes and they taught me dynamics how to phrase these notes and how to do these things just play them straight and that's the way they helped me how to do these things
where would they help you you know where did they you sit down you took
your horns
out
well George you will play this like this you have a crescendo and when they play this crescendo you start at the lowest and come on up and things like that and play dynamics
so they're very helpful
a lot of
times now you don't hear musicians really helping each other out that much or you know everybody's just suspected to show up and play
you know
what I mean but they sound like they took a lot of time out to show you exactly what to do

yes they did yes even on the boat a lot of time I went to him for help he was a very good man he had very good musician who is this Louis Nelson and his breathing he was very good in the method of breathing he was a very good trombone player and during the time of Tommy Doss's Eerie when he was playing he was playing when Tommy Dossie played the high notes on the trombone well he would play that even on the boat he would play that we was working
Louis Nelson could play those
things yes yes
because the way Louis Nelson plays now it's very broad and he plays fairly kind of in the middle range of the trombone he doesn't play up there a lot now

well he did a lot of Tommy Doss's arrangements a lot of Tommy Doss's he did that and with ease he used to sit on and just broom right out in the head like a megaphone during that time the trombone player used to blow in a big megaphone quiet the tone down it wouldn't be so brassy he would get there during that time trumpet players had derbies on the stand and you had mutes that you used during that time for different effects I don't see them maybe in the big bands now they might still use these type of mutes
what you mentioned Louie Nelson's technique of breathing what was that what did he tell you about breathing

well he told me that his teacher the one I don't remember his name he took the lesson from told him the important thing of playing that horn is to learn how to breathe and that is from the diaphragm and by the high notes he used to hit it was from the diaphragm and not from the lip and it took a long time for me to understand because mine was more lip power than it was any other method that's the only weapon I knew
yeah well most people when they start out playing they think it's all in the lips right
well during that time you had to get a corn on your lip as I understand before you could play so I was working toward that corn on my lip
you had to get a corn
on your lip yeah it's a corn and I used to see these corn where they they trim them with a razor blade I've seen a guy actually trim the corn on his lip with a razor blade
so he thought he was playing right because he had a corn yeah

I guess so because he played so much this guy was oh he was great he was one and he his playing he made he record he made a record with Joe Robichaud who's that Gene Ware he made a record with Joe Robichaud about 19 well he could have been about 1929 or 30 could have been around that time
yeah

could have been a little later but he's on that Joe Robichaud record they went to New York the band was so good they were jealous of him in New York and they wouldn't let him record anymore really oh they had some good guys in that band they were really good good band
what else did Louie Nelson talk to you about he told you about breathing and how to read
he also gave me a lot of pointers about life I was about 19 or 20 years old at that
time

and he told me the do's and the don'ts narcotics was one don't fool with narcotics yeah and I never did have fool with he told me don't ever fool around with that and be careful you're youngster and you had a long ways to go Sidney Desvien was instrumental in helping me in that direction yeah in fact a lot of guys in the band I was the youngest guy in the band
yeah
and all of them was
what did they tell you about women George
well always love women they say well be careful be careful and try to pick the nice ones instead of the bad ones
yeah I'm sorry what did you say George

I used to my dad used to take me to the old lyrics theater in New Orleans that was the kingdom of all the wonderful entertainers like Bessie Smith I saw Bessie Smith when I was a little bit of boy and they had a lot of old musicians used to play during that time in the pit yeah and so that had a lot to do with me I've only heard
her you know naturally on record and they
say
the record doesn't do Bessie Smith justice I mean when she came out and sang was it pretty powerful

yeah oh she was a powerful singer and then Bessie they had Mamie they had Ma Rainey they had Ida Cox oh they had and Ethel Waters used to sing a lot of blues too before she went into the religious field she was a good singer
so they'd all come through and do big stage performances
yeah all that went through by the came to the lyrics theater at one time okay
so anyhow you're out you're out on the boats there you're on the steamer capital and Louie Nelson's giving you lessons that's pretty good
sounds pretty good
and Eugene where
Sydney Desvane was had
you know given me a lot of did you only have to work about an hour a day out on the boat

when I we started oh at the beginning we only played we rehearsed during the day up on the way to St. Paul Minnesota down in Mississippi and on the way up to Missouri and Ohio not Ohio but Iowa during that time we rehearsed during the day and we played one trip that was from 8 to 12 at night during the dance but when you got to St. Paul Minnesota when we got up there we started at 9 o'clock in the morning until 5 o'clock in the evening and we came back at 8 o'clock that night until 12 o'clock that night must have got your chops in shape the first year it was rough the first year it was really rough to
Thank you.
So the first year was rough.

Well I had lip infection because I wasn't brewing properly and trying to imitate the trumpet player was so great and I admired him so much was Gene Ware. He blew on the side of his mouth and he could triple tongue so fast but his tongue was protruding his lips and going into the mouthpiece to the point where he had worn a sort of a crease in his lip. Really? And therefore he used to have a corn on there and he used to shave this corn with a razor blade. I've seen him cut this corn off, trim it down. But he was so great and so by me, my tongue used to pass my teeth and my lip it wore a little raw spot there and this got infected and I didn't just kept going. But the next year was better. Next year was much better. I tried to correct my mistakes. In fact I did and I didn't have that problem.
So who was playing on the boats within those years? Who else was in the band?
I had Bostic, Earl Bostic, the late Earl Bostic. Yeah.
Yeah.

And the, well I'll start from the trumpet section. There was Sidney Dazman, Eugene Ware and I. Three trumpets, Lewis Nelson was on trombone. And I go from the sax section. There was Earl Bostic and there was Eugene Hall. He's playing, I think he's still living in San Diego. And there was, I had three saxophones and, oh yeah, Gishard. A little Gishard. How do you spell that name? G-I-S-S-E-R-D Gishard.
And his first name? What was his first name? He said Little. It must have been a little and a big one.
No, that was Big Gish because they had Little Gish played bass. They were two brothers. Yeah. And the one they called Little Gish and the other one Big Gish.
Everybody in New Orleans has nicknames. I've always noticed that. What was your nickname on the boats? Cuz. Cuz. Why'd they call you Cuz? C-U-Z-Z? C-U-Z-Z. Yeah.
I had Cuz because I used to call everybody Cousin. Yeah. And if I didn't know your name, I'd say, hi Cuz. So, that was pleasant to see everybody accepted as such.
Yeah. Well, I guess Louie called everybody Pops.

A lot of people did. Yeah. So, he used to call, had a nickname for people, you know. But during my younger years, they had names of prize fighters and great trumpet players. Had the same kid. They used to call him like Kid Rennie or Kid Shots. Yeah. Those in the prize fighters were kids also.
Yeah. I've always liked that about New Orleans. Everybody seems to have a nickname in New Orleans. Everybody you meet down there has got a nickname. So, there you were on the boat with the band.
Now, Lewis Nelson. Lewis Nelson's nickname was Doyle. What? Doyle. D-O-Y-L-E. Doyle.
Why would they call him Doyle?
I don't know, but that was his nickname.

That's pretty good. And Earl Bostick, did he have a nickname? Bosto. Bosto? Bosto. We call him Bosto. Yeah. That's pretty good. So, I mean, there were you guys. What actually happened on the boats? Did people stay overnight or did they just get on on a particular place and ride up the river for a while and dance? Was it?
No. No. It was a moonlight dance like they'd get off right after the dance.
So, you'd go back to the same landing port.

Up there, it was one-nighters. Right. Every night, we played in a different city or a little place and they would come on at eight and leave at twelve. I see. So, the only thing that stayed on the boat was the crew.
I see. Musicians and the crew. I see. So, there weren't a lot of passengers. No, no, there were no passengers. Um, so what tunes did you play with that band? Trumpet. Now, what tunes did you play?
Oh, with the Sydney Desvind band? Yeah. Uh, we played a lot of modern stuff during that time. All the tunes in the thirties. Uh, you got the tune? Yeah. Check it out.
Yeah. Check it out.

Yeah. We had, um, Blue Prelude. We played that. And, uh, did you ever see a dream go walking? Don't blame me. And, um, they had a lot of tunes. I covered the waterfront. And, uh, Tommy Darcy, this tune that, uh, Lewis Nelson used to play, I'm getting sentimental over you. Yeah. He played that jazz like Tommy Johnson. Really? The tone and everything was just beautiful. And, um, we had a lot of, uh, this, the, the captain of the, of the steamship, he belonged to ASCAP. I think that was the name of the recording, uh, ASCAP at that time. And he used to get the, uh, the sheet music right off the press. And a lot of times the Streck was steamship, uh, Lionhead, what's playing that music before the average man start playing it. Oh, because he was in ASCAP. Oh, yes.
The captain liked the music? Oh, yes. Who was the captain of the boat? Oh.
Roy Streckfus was the captain of, uh, of the Steamer Capital.
How's he spelled his name? R-O-Y. Yeah.
S-T-R-U-C-K-F-U-S. Streckfus. Say that one more time, George. Roy Streckfus.
Yeah. Spell the last name.
S-T-R-U-C-K-F-U-S. Uh-huh.
So he really liked the music, the captain, uh...

Yes, he was a violin player. Uh-huh. And, uh, he liked the music. He liked it very well. And, uh... Did he sit in? And, uh, they would always practically give you the repertoire to play beside the other stuff you had. But, uh, most of the music that was coming out at that time, the sheet music, was issued to you, to the band, and they would play that at that time. Well, it'd become, uh, to a part where this band could play, uh, music right straight down as you give us this music without a rehearsal. We'd just go in and play it.
Was he, was the captain sort of like the manager of the ballroom? I mean, was he as much involved with running the band as he was running the ship? Yes.

Yes. To a certain extent. Uh, he would, uh, tell you what tempos to play. Uh-huh. And, uh, we had, say, eighteen dances during that time. The dances was in sets. You played so many dances to a set. And then the next number, number two. And then, uh, maybe number three dance, we had a waltz to play in there. Well, if you didn't time it just right, like so many beats, uh, uh, to the minute, uh, to the bar, something like that, and you didn't time it just right, well, you wouldn't come out on that eighteen dances in time. Yes. Yes. So you had to time these numbers. And so you, uh, Sidney used to look at his watch and see how many, how many beats you were doing in that minute. Really? And by, uh, uh, timing that beats that minute, you can tell how many beats you were giving this piece. If you would give it a little bit faster, then you would be over. And so you had to come out exactly on that eighteen, because, uh, a lot of people say, well, I'll dance with you on dance number five. Well, dance number five had to come up at a certain time, and they'd be waiting for that dance. Oh, really? Yes. So it really was precise. Yeah. A lot of that was.
Now, uh, so you played on the boats for how long? Uh, I played that season, uh, 1933. Uh-huh.

And, uh, we left, uh, St. Paul, Minnesota, where I was up in St. Paul, Minnesota. We left New Orleans and went right up the river. Every town and every city, uh, on the Mississippi River we played. Until we got to St. Paul, Minnesota, that was about in, uh, July. Let's see, June, July, about the middle of July. And then, uh, uh, that was the end of the season, began to get cold up in St. Paul. And then, uh, uh, uh, that was the end of the season, began to get cold up in St. Paul. Yeah. And the boat, it did head back. The band does not play. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
